#Creating a function that takes the parameters required to run a logistic growth model and returns a dataframe with columns for population size and time.
# Inputs: N0 = initial population size.
# r = intrinsic growth rate 
# K = carrying capacity
# tfinal = ending time for simulation
# tstep  = time step increment
# Output: A dataframe with any time between 1:100 with intervals of 5
# popsize = population size at each time
#########################################################################


log_growth <- function(N0=40, r=0.1, K=100, tfinal=100, tstep=5) {
# time sequence from 0 to tfinal by tstep
times <- seq(from=0, to=tfinal, by=tstep)
  
# logistic growth equation

popsize <- K / (1 + ((K - N0) / N0) * exp(-r * times))
  
# dataframe for plotting
df_loggrowth <- data.frame(times=times, popsize=popsize)
# return the dataframe
return(df_loggrowth)

}

For question 1. I asked if life expectancy improve over time at different rates across continents? Hypothesis: Life expectancy rises over time, but the pattern of that increase varies by continent. Using the gapminder dataset, I investigated whether temporal changes in life expectancy differed across continents. A linear mixed model was chosen since life expectancy is a continuous variable and the dataset contains repeated measurements from the same countries over several years. To address this repeated-measures structure, country was included as a random effect. A year-by-continent interaction term was also added to assess whether the rate of change over time varied between continents. The model results indicate that Africa (the reference continent) showed a baseline increase of approximately 0.29 years of life expectancy per year since 1950. The Americas and Asia exhibited significantly faster rates of improvement, with additional gains of roughly 0.08 and 0.16 years per year respectively, while Europe and Oceania showed slightly slower rates of increase compared to Africa. The ANOVA confirmed that year, continent, and their interaction were all highly significant (p < 0.05), meaning the rate of change in life expectancy over time was not the same across all continents. This supports the hypothesis that life expectancy trends are continent-dependent rather than following a single, consistent global trajectory.

To investigate this, I used the gapminder dataset to examine whether population trajectories over time differed across continents. A negative binomial generalized linear mixed model was selected given that population is a heavily right-skewed, non-Gaussian variable, which makes a standard linear model unsuitable. As in the previous analysis, country was included as a random effect to account for repeated observations per country. A year-by-continent interaction term was also incorporated to capture whether temporal population trends varied between continents. The reference continent, Africa, showed a baseline population growth rate of approximately 0.025 per year since 1950. library(deSolve)


#####################################################
# FUNCTION: run_sir_model
# PURPOSE: Solve deterministic SIR model with deSolve
# INPUTS:
#   beta, gamma : transmission & recovery rates
#   N           : total population
#   S0, I0, R0  : initial conditions
#   t_start     : start time
#   t_end       : end time
#   dt          : timestep
# OUTPUT:
#   data.frame with columns: time, S, I, R
##########################################
# The function below solves the SIR model for a single parameter set and will be used inside your loops to conduct the parameter sweep.

run_sir_model <- function(
  beta    = 0.1,
  gamma   = 0.1,
  N       = 1000,
  S0      = 999,
  I0      = 1,
  R0      = 0,
  t_start = 0,
  t_end   = 160,
  dt      = 1
) {

  init  <- c(S = S0, I = I0, R = R0)
  times <- seq(t_start, t_end, by = dt)

  sir_equations <- function(time, state, parameters) {
    with(as.list(c(state, parameters)), {
      dS <- -beta * S * I / N
      dI <-  beta * S * I / N - gamma * I
      dR <-  gamma * I
      list(c(dS, dI, dR))
    })
  }

  out <- ode(
    y     = init,
    times = times,
    func  = sir_equations,
    parms = c(beta = beta, gamma = gamma, N = N)
  )

  as.data.frame(out)
}

##############################################################
# END FUNCTION


# creating parameter vectors

gamma_vec <- seq(from = 0, to = 0.5, by = 0.01)

# start of function "sir_param_sweep"

sir_param_sweep <- function(
    beta_params,
    gamma_params
){
    
    ##### Creating storage df:
    ## finding the length of the df
    df <- length(beta_params)*length(gamma_params)

    ## creating each column in the df
    beta_out <- rep(NA, df)
    gamma_out <- rep(NA, df)
    max_infected <- rep(NA, df)

    ## creating the df
    storage_df <- data.frame(beta_out, gamma_out, max_infected)

    counter <- 1

    for(i in seq_along(beta_params)){
        for(j in seq_along(gamma_params)){

            # run sir model
            temp_df <- run_sir_model(beta = beta_params[i], gamma = gamma_params[j])

            # store variables inside df
            storage_df$max_infected[counter] <- max(temp_df$I)
            storage_df$beta_out[counter] <- beta_params[i]
            storage_df$gamma_out[counter] <- gamma_params[j]

            # increasing the counter
            counter <- counter + 1
            }
        }

  return(storage_df)

}
